strengths: Significant community contribution: a large, curated, real-world benchmark spanning eight CO problems (MIS, MDS, TSP, CVRP, CFLP, CPMP, FJSP, STP) sourced from DIMACS, TSPLib, PACE, and other competition/industrial repositories, with test instances orders of magnitude larger than prior ML4CO evaluations (TSP up to 10M nodes, MIS up to 8M nodes).

Careful and standardized evaluation infrastructure: standardized BKS for all test instances (collected from literature/leaderboards and validated with SOTA solvers on the authors' servers), standardized training/validation sets, a data loader/evaluation toolkit with leakage protection, and a unified primal-gap metric, all of which address well-known reproducibility problems in ML4CO research.

Comprehensive cross-paradigm evaluation: 16 representative neural solvers and LLM-based agents compared against problem-specific SOTA classical solvers under a uniform 1-hour budget, with a clear easy/hard split separating 'historically hard but now solvable' from 'open/structurally hard' instances.

Genuinely informative analyses beyond raw rankings: ablations showing the neural module helps only weak base heuristics (DIFUSCO vs 2-OPT, GCNN vs SCIP), the Euclidean vs non-Euclidean STP experiment exposing GNNs' reliance on locality, the efficiency analysis showing LKH-3 fast-mode dominates neural fast-mode, and the word-cloud analysis of LLM-discovered algorithms showing they replicate known metaheuristics (SA, LNS).

Honest and useful headline findings: ML solvers lag classical SOTA far more than prior papers suggested, with quantified distribution-shift effects (e.g., LEHD's 0.72% gap on synthetic TSP becoming 10%/77% on easy/hard real-world sets).
weaknesses: Several suspicious data entries undermine confidence in the experiments: in Table 11 (STP), RL and SL have identical gaps and times to the second decimal on both easy and hard sets, suggesting a copy/reporting error; in Table 8 (CFLP-hard), tMDP, SORREL, and GCNN all report exactly 55.35±21.7%; DeepACO's hard-set time (3333s) deviates unexplained from the protocol. These need verification or correction.

Fairness concerns in the headline claims: the central 'persistent performance gap' conclusion is partly an artifact of design—neural solvers are evaluated with official checkpoints trained on small synthetic distributions against instances 3–4 orders of magnitude larger, so severe degradation is largely expected rather than a discovery; no retraining/fine-tuning on the provided FrontierCO training data is reported, which weakens the generality of the 'ML falls short' narrative.

The claim that LLM agents 'outperform SOTA classical solvers' is overdrawn: Self-Refine beating KaMIS on easy MIS (1.30% vs 1.51%, with ±3.89% std over ~36 instances) is within noise, and the paper itself admits these agents implement known sophisticated heuristics (kernelization, Tomita-style clique, ARW, ILS with VND) discovered via expensive iterative search—so this is LLM-driven re-implementation of literature methods, not a new solver capability; results are also tied to one specific model (o4-mini).

Test sets are small (roughly 10–36 instances per problem/difficulty) and highly heterogeneous in scale, so mean primal gaps have huge variance (e.g., 77%±34% on TSP-hard), yet conclusions are drawn from aggregate means without per-instance or significance analysis in the main text; the infeasible=>gap=1 convention conflates 'failed to run' with 'poor solution quality' in the averages.

Classical baselines are uneven: for MDS, CFLP, and FJSP the paper uses general-purpose Gurobi/CPLEX rather than the strongest problem-specific heuristics (the paper itself cites a CP-based Benders method as strongest for FJSP but omits it due to unavailable code), so 'SOTA classical solver' comparisons are not uniformly SOTA.

Novelty is primarily in curation rather than methodology, and positioning relative to very recent competing benchmarks (ML4CO-bench-101, RL4CO, CO-Bench, ML4TSPBench) is discussed only briefly without a comparative feature table or head-to-head differentiation.

Reproducibility is claimed but incomplete: the benchmark URL in the abstract and the code link in the reproducibility statement are blank in the manuscript, and some appendix checkpoint/footnote links are empty; key details such as instance-level BKS values, per-instance results, and exact hardware configurations for the LLM iterations would be needed for full replication.

Minor presentation issues: the metric section's handling of maximization-to-minimization conversion for MIS vs. the primal gap definition could confuse readers; Figure 2 log-scale bars with infeasibility asterisks are hard to interpret precisely; the LLM variance analysis (Section 4, 'Fourth') is largely speculative hypothesis without supporting variance measurements.

strengths: Ambitious scope: eight CO problems spanning routing, scheduling, facility location, graph, and tree problems, with instances drawn from authoritative sources (TSPLib, DIMACS, PACE, BHOSLib, SteinLib, OR-Brescia), pushing to orders-of-magnitude larger scales (TSP up to 10M nodes, MIS up to 8M) than prior ML evaluations.

Useful infrastructure contribution: standardized BKS for all test instances, standardized training/validation data, a toolkit with data loader/evaluation function/LLM solving template, and an explicit easy/hard set design that guards against 'heuristic hacking' of memorized solutions.

Breadth of evaluation: 16 representative ML solvers across three paradigms (end-to-end neural, MIP-guided learning, LLM agents) evaluated under a unified protocol against genuine SOTA classical solvers (LKH-3, KaMIS, HGS, Gurobi, CPLEX, SCIP-Jack).

Several analysis sections go beyond leaderboard reporting: ablation on whether the neural module helps (Table 3), the Euclidean vs. non-Euclidean GNN experiment (Figure 3), efficiency analysis of fast-mode configurations (Table 12), and an additional ATSP study that usefully shows difficulty is not purely a function of size.
Honest high-level conclusions: the paper does not oversell ML for CO and correctly identifies scalability, OOM failures, distribution shift, and LLM variance as core open problems.
weaknesses: Presentation and data-integrity issues undermine confidence: the benchmark URL and code URL are blank ('available at .'), Table 1 appears to have the MIS easy/hard node ranges swapped (easy set lists 1.4M–8M nodes, hard set 1,150–4,000), RL and SL rows in Table 11 are numerically identical, and timing entries are malformed ('1347 ±× 1.63 s'). For a benchmark paper, where the artifact is the contribution, this level of sloppiness is disqualifying without a careful revision.

The headline finding—that ML solvers trained on synthetic data degrade under distribution shift and scale—is largely an artifact of the evaluation setup rather than a new scientific result. Most neural solvers are run with official checkpoints trained on different distributions (e.g., DIFUSCO on TSP-10000, SIL on TSP-1000) instead of being retrained on the benchmark's own standardized training sets. Given the authors provide standardized training data, the fairer (and more informative) experiment of retraining each method on it is conspicuously missing; without it, the 77% TSP gap claim conflates method limitations with avoidable deployment choices.

Limited novelty of conclusions: that GNNs underperform classical greedy/heuristic methods on non-Euclidean graph problems was already established (e.g., Angelini & Ricci-Tersenghi, 2022; Böther et al., 2022), and 'ML lags SOTA on real instances' is widely suspected; the value rests almost entirely on benchmark construction, which makes the reproducibility and correctness issues above more damaging.

The 'LLM-based agents outperform SOTA classical solvers' claim is overstated. The mechanism described (Self-Refine applies kernelization, Tomita-style max-clique, ARW-style heuristics with crossover and path-relinking; FunSearch builds ILS with regret insertion and VND) means these are essentially hand-engineered classical metaheuristics scaffolded by an LLM, and the LLM-agents receive 64 dev-set feedback iterations plus a 3600s test budget while classical solvers get a single 1-hour run—an unclear and arguably unfair compute accounting.

Statistical reporting is thin: primal gaps are averaged over very small instance sets (e.g., 10–19 hard instances, 10 CVRP hard instances), some with enormous variance (±45.57%, ±41.06%), and several conclusions rest on single-digit-instance aggregates; the treatment of infeasible runs as gap=1 further distorts means in ways not analyzed.

Positioning against closely related concurrent benchmarks (ML4CO-bench-101, ML4TSPBench, RL4CO, CO-Bench) is superficial; the paper does not clearly articulate what is uniquely enabled by FrontierCO relative to these, beyond size.

Some results are confusing or under-analyzed: identical CFLP hard-set gaps for tMDP/SORREL/GCNN (55.35%), FunSearch achieving exactly 0.00% on ATSP-easy while timing out at 3600s, and the STP neural baselines (RL/SL) being far behind LLM agents without discussion.

strengths: Significant and timely contribution: the paper addresses a genuine and well-documented gap in ML4CO evaluation—reliance on small, synthetic, distribution-matched benchmarks—by curating real competition-grade instances (DIMACS, TSPLib, PACE, BHOSLib, etc.) at extreme scale (TSP up to 10M nodes, MIS up to 8M).

Broad and well-structured benchmark design: eight CO problems spanning five categories, with a thoughtful easy/hard split that separates 'historically hard but now solvable' instances from genuinely open or structurally adversarial ones, reducing susceptibility to 'heuristic hacking' and memorization.

Impressive unified evaluation effort: 16 ML solvers across neural, hybrid, and LLM-agentic paradigms, evaluated against state-of-the-art classical solvers (KaMIS, LKH-3, HGS, Gurobi, CPLEX, SCIP-Jack) under a standardized protocol, with standardized BKS and training/validation data—this alone is a valuable community resource.

The paper goes beyond benchmarking to deliver substantive empirical insights: (i) a careful ablation (Table 3) showing neural modules help weak baselines but not strong ones, (ii) a novel controlled experiment (Section 5.2, Figure 3) demonstrating that GNNs fail to learn on non-Euclidean STP instances, pointing to a fundamental locality limitation, and (iii) analysis of LLM-generated algorithms (Figure 4, Section 5.3) showing LLM agents rediscover classical metaheuristics rather than inventing new ones—an important, honest characterization.

Highly detailed reproducibility documentation: appendices cover data provenance with URLs, checkpoint configurations, prompt templates, and compute settings; the efficiency analysis (Appendix E) and ATSP extension (Appendix F) strengthen the rigor of the evaluation.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to existing benchmarks (RL4CO, ML4TSPBench, CO-Bench, ML4CO-bench-101, Jumanji). The main advance is scale and instance realism rather than a new evaluation methodology; the related-work positioning against these prior benchmarks could be sharper about what is genuinely new.

Fairness of the cross-paradigm comparison is questionable in places: neural solvers use fixed public checkpoints trained on distributions quite different from the test instances (severe distribution shift is then reported as a key finding—somewhat circular), while LLM agents get 64 iterations of development on a provided validation set plus full 3600s test runs. The claim that 'LLM-based solvers may outperform SOTA classical solvers' is somewhat misleading: closer inspection reveals Self-Refine essentially re-implements classical kernelization + ARW-style heuristics, so this is more 'LLMs can write known classical algorithms' than a fundamental capability claim.

Several reported numbers raise reproducibility concerns: the RL and SL STP baselines show identical gaps, times, and standard deviations in Table 11 (14.00 ± 3.31 / 13.10 ± 6.52), and tMDP, SORREL, and GCNN show identical hard-set results on CFLP (55.35 ± 21.7)—these appear to be copy-paste errors or unexplained degenerate cases that need clarification.

No statistical treatment of the LLM agents' high variance: the paper itself notes LLM-based solvers 'display high variance,' yet reports single runs (apparently) without multiple seeds or confidence intervals, which undermines conclusions like FunSearch outperforming HGS on hard CVRP.
The benchmark URL in the abstract and reproducibility statement is blank ('available at .'), so the availability of the central artifact cannot be verified at review time.

Compute-cost equivalence is not addressed: one LLM agent run involves 64 o4-mini iterations plus API costs that are not comparable to a 1-hour single-core CPU or single-GPU budget; Appendix G acknowledges deployment cost differences qualitatively but the headline comparisons treat all budgets as equivalent.

Coverage asymmetries: several neural method categories are thinly covered per problem (e.g., only RL/SL baselines for STP, no neural solver for MDS-hard due to OOM), and the training data description explicitly omits 'number of instances and parameter settings,' weakening reproducibility for the neural side.
